summary: Discusses three views of byte size for network connections: it should not be used at all, it is only for the NCP's convenience, or it is a user-level choice. The authors explain why the first view was dropped during the Host-Host protocol cleanup in RFC 107.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC discusses whether network connections should use fixed-size bytes and who should choose that size. The authors favor letting user-level protocols specify it, while leaving the wider bit-stream question for later review.

subtitle: Three views on who should choose a connection's byte size.

tldr.problem: RFC 107 left open who should choose a connection's byte size: the NCP or the user-level process.
tldr.mechanism: The authors compare three views and argue that a user process should be able to specify the size, while third-level protocols may set a fixed size where useful.
tldr.outcome: The RFC recommends leaving the broader bit-stream versus byte-stream question for a major Host-Host Protocol review.

sections.title: Three Views of Byte Size
sections.content:
The RFC describes three views: connections should be bit streams with no byte size, byte size should be chosen only for NCP convenience, or users should control byte size. The first view had been set aside in favor of byte streams for reasons of storage-management and message-concatenation efficiency.

Under the third view, a process may choose a byte size explicitly or implicitly through its input/output mode. An NCP may use a default when the process makes no choice.
sections.plainLanguage: The debate is about who chooses the size of each unit of data. The authors favor letting the program using the connection choose, or use a default when it does not specify one.

sections.title: Why User-Level Choice Matters
sections.content:
The authors say RFC 107 treats byte-size choice as a third-level protocol issue. TELNET and the Initial Connection Protocol (ICP) require particular byte sizes, so their user-level processes need to be able to specify that choice to the NCP.

If the NCP alone chooses, the byte size can mismatch both between communicating NCPs and between an NCP and its user process.
sections.plainLanguage: A protocol that needs a particular byte size should be able to request it. Otherwise, its data may not fit the size chosen below it.

sections.title: When Protocols Fix a Byte Size
sections.content:
The RFC gives two arguments for fixing a byte size in a third-level protocol. RFC 107 does not require every NCP to support every size from 1 through 255, while 8-bit sizes or multiples of 8 are acceptable to all hosts, including terminal IMPs. A known size may also reduce program space and possibly running time.

TELNET data consists of 8-bit ASCII characters, and ICP carries 32-bit socket numbers. Data-transfer protocols are less straightforward: a fixed size can reduce efficiency when the data has another structure, and filler fields may be needed. The size also stays fixed for the connection's life.
sections.plainLanguage: A fixed size can make some protocols simpler and more efficient. It can also waste space when the data naturally uses a different size.

sections.title: Reopening the Bit-Stream Question
sections.content:
The discussion questions whether byte streams gained enough overall efficiency to justify losing the generality of bit streams. It says the combined efficiency of user processes and NCPs matters more than NCP efficiency alone.

The authors recommend setting the issue aside until a major Host-Host Protocol overhaul can examine it.
sections.plainLanguage: The authors are not sure byte streams improve efficiency overall. They recommend revisiting that question during a broader protocol review.
